Four species with widespread ranges are fishes whose restoration will be limited first by availability of suitable waters. Lakes and streams in which the shortnose sturgeon, lake sturgeon, Arctic grayling and Colorado squawfish were originally found flowed from watersheds in a number of North American biomes. It is uncertain, but probably unlikely, that these waters were characteristic alone of the biomes from which they flowed. Restoration will be possible in few of the waters in which they originally lived.
The foregoing species and subspecies are those likely to appear on the first list of endangered species prepared under provisions of the proposed legislation which are widespread in distribution and whose successful restoration, therefore, will have more far reaching effects on the environment of the United States. Most of these animals are rather loosely identified with biomes in which they are and once were found. Approximately one-third of the species and subspecies are dependent for their survival and restoration upon special features within the biome such as water. Few of the animals may be considered to have been among the dominants in their association or even closely associated with their biome.
Geographical isolation: Populations that become sufficiently isolated from others of the species to develop identifiable characteristics of their own may become recognized as a new and separate subspecies. The barrier that prevents intergradation of two subspecies of the same species may be as simple as an intervening ridge between two watersheds or a narrow band of hostile environment.
